chapterTitle: Soldier, Athlete, Farmer, Workman — Pass It On and Rightly Handle the Word
themeTitle: “The Things Which You Have Heard From Me … Commit the Same to Faithful Men”

scripture.text: You therefore, my child, be strengthened in the grace that is in Christ Jesus.
scripture.understanding: σὺ οὖν, τέκνον μου, “You therefore, my child” — in contrast to the deserters of 1:15 — ἐνδυναμοῦ, “be strengthened” — ἐνδυναμόω from the power family: be continually empowered from within — ἐν τῇ χάριτι, “in the grace that is in Christ Jesus.” Strength for ministry does not come from willpower but from grace. The command is passive: let yourself be strengthened.

scripture.text: The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also.
scripture.understanding: The great relay verse: “The things which you have heard (ἤκουσας) from me among many witnesses (μαρτύρων), commit (παράθου — deposit, entrust) the same to faithful (πιστοῖς) men, who will be able (ἱκανοί — competent, qualified) to teach (διδάξαι) others also.” Four generations: Paul, Timothy, faithful people, others. The gospel spreads through people who receive it, live it and pass it on. Faithfulness comes before ability.

scripture.text: You therefore must endure hardship, as a good soldier of Christ Jesus.
scripture.understanding: The first picture: the soldier. συγκακοπάθησον, “endure hardship” — share in suffering (the WEB follows manuscripts reading simply ‘endure hardship’) — ὡς καλὸς στρατιώτης Χριστοῦ Ἰησοῦ, “as a good soldier of Christ Jesus.” καλός from the good family: a fine, excellent soldier. Soldiers expect hardship; it comes with the uniform.

scripture.text: No soldier on duty entangles himself in the affairs of life, that he may please him who enrolled him as a soldier.
scripture.understanding: “No soldier on duty (στρατευόμενος) entangles himself (ἐμπλέκεται — gets wrapped up, tangled) in the affairs (πραγματείαις) of life (βίου).” βίος from the life family: the business of everyday earthly life — trade, possessions, civilian concerns. A soldier on campaign is not forbidden to eat or sleep, but he does not get tangled in business that distracts from his mission, ἵνα τῷ στρατολογήσαντι ἀρέσῃ, “that he may please him who enrolled him as a soldier.” The question is not ‘Is this allowed?’ but ‘Does this entangle me?’

scripture.text: Also, if anyone competes in athletics, he isn’t crowned unless he has competed by the rules.
scripture.understanding: The second picture: the athlete. ἐὰν δὲ καὶ ἀθλῇ τις, “Also, if anyone competes in athletics,” οὐ στεφανοῦται, “he isn’t crowned” — the victor's wreath — ἐὰν μὴ νομίμως ἀθλήσῃ, “unless he has competed by the rules.” At the Olympic games, athletes swore to train for ten months and compete fairly; cheaters were disqualified. Christian ministry has rules too: faithfulness, truth, integrity. Shortcuts forfeit the crown.

scripture.text: The farmer who labors must be the first to get a share of the crops.
scripture.understanding: The third picture: the farmer. τὸν κοπιῶντα γεωργόν, “The farmer who labors” — κοπιάω from the work family: toil to exhaustion — δεῖ πρῶτον τῶν καρπῶν μεταλαμβάνειν, “must be the first to get a share of the crops.” The hard-working farmer rightly enjoys the harvest first. Patient, wearying labour in God's field will be rewarded.

scripture.text: Consider what I say, and may the Lord give you understanding in all things.
scripture.understanding: νόει ὃ λέγω, “Consider what I say” — think it through, reflect on the pictures. δώσει γάρ σοι ὁ κύριος σύνεσιν ἐν πᾶσιν, “and may the Lord give you understanding in all things” — σύνεσις, insight that puts things together. Thinking and prayer belong together: we reflect, and the Lord gives understanding.

scripture.text: Remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, of the offspring of David, according to my Good News,
scripture.understanding: μνημόνευε Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν ἐγηγερμένον ἐκ νεκρῶν, “Remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead” — ἐγείρω from the rise family, perfect tense: raised and still alive. ἐκ σπέρματος Δαυίδ, “of the offspring of David” — the promised Messiah-King. This, Paul says, is κατὰ τὸ εὐαγγέλιόν μου, “according to my Good News.” In suffering, the most important thing to remember is not a principle but a Person: the risen King.

scripture.text: in which I suffer hardship to the point of chains as a criminal. But God’s word isn’t chained.
scripture.understanding: For this gospel Paul κακοπαθῶ, “suffers hardship,” μέχρι δεσμῶν ὡς κακοῦργος, “to the point of chains as a criminal” — κακοῦργος, ‘evil-worker’, the word used of the criminals crucified with Jesus (Luke 23:32). “But God’s word (λόγος) isn’t chained (δέδεται).” The messenger can be bound; the message cannot. Paul's letters from prison prove it.

scripture.text: Therefore I endure all things for the chosen ones’ sake, that they also may obtain the salvation which is in Christ Jesus with eternal glory.
scripture.understanding: “Therefore I endure (ὑπομένω — remain under, bear up) all things for the chosen ones’ sake (ἐκλεκτούς),” so that they also τύχωσιν, “may obtain,” τῆς σωτηρίας, “the salvation which is in Christ Jesus with eternal glory (δόξης αἰωνίου).” Paul's suffering serves God's people: through it the gospel reaches those God has chosen. Election does not make mission unnecessary; it makes mission certain of fruit.

scripture.text: This saying is trustworthy: “For if we died with him, we will also live with him.
scripture.understanding: The fourth ‘faithful saying’ (πιστὸς ὁ λόγος), probably an early hymn in four lines. Line one: “For if we died with him (συναπεθάνομεν), we will also live with him (συζήσομεν).” The συν- prefix, ‘with’, ties believers to Christ: united with Him in His death (Romans 6:8), we share His life.

scripture.text: If we endure, we will also reign with him. If we deny him, he also will deny us.
scripture.understanding: Line two: “If we endure (ὑπομένομεν), we will also reign with him (συμβασιλεύσομεν).” Endurance now leads to sharing Christ's reign. Line three, a solemn warning, using ἀρνέομαι, to deny or disown: “If we deny him, he also will deny us” (v. 12) — echoing Jesus' words in Matthew 10:33. Persistent, final denial of Christ has eternal consequences.

scripture.text: If we are faithless, he remains faithful. For he can’t deny himself.”
scripture.understanding: Line four breaks the pattern: εἰ ἀπιστοῦμεν, “If we are faithless” — wavering, failing in faith — ἐκεῖνος πιστὸς μένει, “he remains faithful.” Not ‘he will be faithless to us’ but ‘He stays faithful’. ἀρνήσασθαι γὰρ ἑαυτὸν οὐ δύναται, “For he can’t deny himself.” There is a difference between deliberate denial (v. 12) and weak faithlessness (v. 13). Peter wavered and was restored. Christ's faithfulness rests on His own character, not ours.

scripture.text: Remind them of these things, charging them in the sight of the Lord, that they don’t argue about words, to no profit, to the subverting of those who hear.
scripture.understanding: ταῦτα ὑπομίμνῃσκε, “Remind them of these things” — keep reminding — διαμαρτυρόμενος ἐνώπιον τοῦ κυρίου, “charging them in the sight of the Lord,” μὴ λογομαχεῖν, “that they don’t argue about words” — word-battles, the false teachers' habit (1 Timothy 6:4) — ἐπ᾽ οὐδὲν χρήσιμον, “to no profit,” ἐπὶ καταστροφῇ τῶν ἀκουόντων, “to the subverting of those who hear” — καταστροφή, overturning, the root of ‘catastrophe’. Endless verbal battles do not build people up; they knock them down.

scripture.text: Give diligence to present yourself approved by God, a workman who doesn’t need to be ashamed, properly handling the Word of Truth.
scripture.understanding: σπούδασον σεαυτὸν δόκιμον παραστῆσαι τῷ θεῷ, “Give diligence to present yourself approved by God” — δόκιμος, tested and approved, like a coin that has passed the assay. ἐργάτην ἀνεπαίσχυντον, “a workman who doesn’t need to be ashamed” — ἐργάτης from the work family: a labourer whose work stands inspection. ὀρθοτομοῦντα τὸν λόγον τῆς ἀληθείας, “properly handling the Word of Truth” — ὀρθοτομέω means to cut straight, like a road-builder cutting a straight path or a craftsman making a straight cut. Handle Scripture accurately, without twisting it.

scripture.text: But shun empty chatter, for it will go further in ungodliness,
scripture.understanding: τὰς δὲ βεβήλους κενοφωνίας περιΐστασο, “But shun empty chatter” — κενοφωνία, empty sounds (1 Timothy 6:20); περιΐστημι, to step around, avoid. ἐπὶ πλεῖον γὰρ προκόψουσιν ἀσεβείας, “for it will go further in ungodliness” — ἀσέβεια from the godliness family: irreverence. προκόπτω is the word for ‘progress’ (1 Timothy 4:15); empty talk makes progress — in the wrong direction.

scripture.text: and those words will consume like gangrene, of whom is Hymenaeus and Philetus;
scripture.understanding: καὶ ὁ λόγος αὐτῶν ὡς γάγγραινα νομὴν ἕξει, “and those words will consume like gangrene” — γάγγραινα, a spreading ulcer that eats living flesh; νομή, spreading, feeding. False teaching does not stay contained; it spreads and destroys healthy tissue. Two examples: Ὑμέναιος, Hymenaeus (1 Timothy 1:20), and Φίλητος, Philetus.

scripture.text: men who have erred concerning the truth, saying that the resurrection is already past, and overthrowing the faith of some.
scripture.understanding: οἵτινες περὶ τὴν ἀλήθειαν ἠστόχησαν, “men who have erred concerning the truth” — ἀστοχέω, missed the mark (1 Timothy 1:6). Their error: λέγοντες ἀνάστασιν ἤδη γεγονέναι, “saying that the resurrection is already past” — ἀνάστασις from the rise family. Perhaps they taught that resurrection was only spiritual, already experienced at conversion, denying a future bodily resurrection (compare 1 Corinthians 15:12). The result: ἀνατρέπουσιν τήν τινων πίστιν, “overthrowing the faith of some” — turning it upside down.

scripture.text: However God’s firm foundation stands, having this seal, “The Lord knows those who are his,” and, “Let every one who names the name of the Lord depart from unrighteousness.”
scripture.understanding: “However God’s firm (στερεός, solid) foundation (θεμέλιος) stands (ἕστηκεν).” Some faith is overturned, but God's foundation is not. It bears a σφραγίς, “seal,” with two inscriptions. First: “The Lord knows those who are his” (v. 19) — ἔγνω, from the know family's γινώσκω: relational knowledge, as in John 10:14, ‘I know my own’ — echoing Numbers 16:5. Second: “Let every one who names (ὀνομάζων) the name of the Lord depart (ἀποστήτω) from unrighteousness (ἀδικίας)” — ἀδικία from the sin family. God's side: He knows His own. Our side: we turn from sin.

scripture.text: Now in a large house there are not only vessels of gold and of silver, but also of wood and of clay. Some are for honor, and some for dishonor.
scripture.understanding: ἐν μεγάλῃ δὲ οἰκίᾳ, “Now in a large house” — the visible church, or the world — there are σκεύη, “vessels,” χρυσᾶ καὶ ἀργυρᾶ, “of gold and of silver,” ξύλινα καὶ ὀστράκινα, “of wood and of clay.” Some are εἰς τιμήν, “for honor” (used for guests and celebrations), some εἰς ἀτιμίαν, “for dishonor” (used for waste and rubbish). In context, the dishonourable vessels are the false teachers.

scripture.text: If anyone therefore purges himself from these, he will be a vessel for honor, sanctified, and suitable for the master’s use, prepared for every good work.
scripture.understanding: ἐὰν οὖν τις ἐκκαθάρῃ ἑαυτὸν ἀπὸ τούτων, “If anyone therefore purges himself from these” — cleanses thoroughly from these influences — he will be σκεῦος εἰς τιμήν, “a vessel for honor,” ἡγιασμένον, “sanctified,” set apart; εὔχρηστον τῷ δεσπότῃ, “suitable for the master’s use” — useful, ready to hand; εἰς πᾶν ἔργον ἀγαθὸν ἡτοιμασμένον, “prepared for every good work” — ἀγαθός from the good family. What a vessel is made of matters less than whether it is clean.

scripture.text: Flee from youthful lusts; but pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace with those who call on the Lord out of a pure heart.
scripture.understanding: τὰς δὲ νεωτερικὰς ἐπιθυμίας φεῦγε, “Flee from youthful lusts” — not only sexual desire but the passions typical of youth: impatience, love of novelty, pride, argumentativeness. δίωκε δέ, “but pursue” — flee and pursue, as in 1 Timothy 6:11 — δικαιοσύνην, πίστιν, ἀγάπην, εἰρήνην, “righteousness, faith, love, and peace,” and do it in company: “with those who call on the Lord out of a pure (καθαρᾶς) heart.” Godliness is pursued together.

scripture.text: But refuse foolish and ignorant questionings, knowing that they generate strife.
scripture.understanding: τὰς δὲ μωρὰς καὶ ἀπαιδεύτους ζητήσεις παραιτοῦ, “But refuse foolish and ignorant questionings” — μωρός, foolish (the root of ‘moron’); ἀπαίδευτος, uninstructed. εἰδὼς ὅτι γεννῶσι μάχας, “knowing that they generate strife” — μάχη, battles. Some questions are asked not to learn but to fight; they give birth to quarrels.

scripture.text: The Lord’s servant must not quarrel, but be gentle towards all, able to teach, patient,
scripture.understanding: δοῦλον δὲ κυρίου οὐ δεῖ μάχεσθαι, “The Lord’s servant must not quarrel” — δοῦλος from the servant family: a bondservant who belongs wholly to the Lord. Instead: ἤπιον εἶναι πρὸς πάντας, “gentle towards all” (v. 24) — kind, mild (as in 1 Thessalonians 2:7); διδακτικόν, “able to teach” (1 Timothy 3:2); ἀνεξίκακον, “patient” — literally ‘enduring evil’, putting up with wrong without resentment.

scripture.text: in gentleness correcting those who oppose him: perhaps God may give them repentance leading to a full knowledge of the truth,
scripture.understanding: ἐν πρᾳΰτητι παιδεύοντα τοὺς ἀντιδιατιθεμένους, “in gentleness correcting those who oppose him” — παιδεύω, to instruct as a parent trains a child. The goal: μήποτε δῴη αὐτοῖς ὁ θεὸς μετάνοιαν, “perhaps God may give them repentance” — repentance is God's gift — εἰς ἐπίγνωσιν ἀληθείας, “leading to a full knowledge of the truth” — ἐπίγνωσις from the know family: full, transforming knowledge. The aim of correction is never to win the argument but to win the person.

scripture.text: and they may recover themselves out of the devil’s snare, having been taken captive by him to his will.
scripture.understanding: καὶ ἀνανήψωσιν, “and they may recover themselves” — literally ‘become sober again’, wake up from spiritual drunkenness — ἐκ τῆς τοῦ διαβόλου παγίδος, “out of the devil’s snare,” ἐζωγρημένοι ὑπ᾽ αὐτοῦ, “having been taken captive by him” — ζωγρέω, to capture alive — εἰς τὸ ἐκείνου θέλημα, “to his will.” Behind false teachers stands a captor. They are not only enemies to be resisted but prisoners to be rescued.

visualMeditations.title: The Relay Race
visualMeditations.image: Picture a relay race. The first runner, old and worn, has carried the baton for miles. His legs are failing, but his grip is firm. He reaches out to the next runner, a young man who has been waiting, and presses the baton into his hand. The young runner sets off, and ahead of him others are already waiting, hands stretched back, ready for their turn. The race is far longer than any one runner's strength. What matters is that the baton is never dropped.
visualMeditations.meaning: “The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also” (v. 2). Paul, Timothy, faithful people, others: four runners in one verse. Paul is about to finish his leg of the race. The gospel survives not through great institutions but through faithful people passing it on, one generation to the next. Someone handed it to you. To whom are you passing it?

visualMeditations.title: Soldier, Athlete, Farmer
visualMeditations.image: Picture three people at dawn. A soldier tightens his belt and marches out, refusing to be distracted by the market stalls and business deals of the town he passes through; his eyes are on his commander. An athlete runs his training laps exactly as the rules require, knowing that a shortcut would disqualify him. A farmer bends over his field in the cold, breaking the soil and sowing seed, his back aching, his harvest months away. Each of them is enduring something hard for something better.
visualMeditations.meaning: “You therefore must endure hardship, as a good soldier of Christ Jesus” (v. 3). The soldier avoids entanglements “that he may please him who enrolled him as a soldier” (v. 4). The athlete “isn’t crowned unless he has competed by the rules” (v. 5). And “The farmer who labors must be the first to get a share of the crops” (v. 6). Faithful service requires focus, integrity and hard work, and each brings its reward. “Consider what I say, and may the Lord give you understanding in all things” (v. 7).

visualMeditations.title: The Straight Cut
visualMeditations.image: Picture a stonemason squaring a block for a temple wall. He measures carefully, marks a line and cuts straight along it. A crooked cut would leave gaps; the wall would be weak and the building would lean. Or picture a road-builder cutting a straight path through a forest so that travellers will not get lost. Now picture a preacher with an open Bible. He can twist the text to fit his opinions, or he can cut straight, letting it say what it says, so that his hearers can walk a straight path to God.
visualMeditations.meaning: “Give diligence to present yourself approved by God, a workman who doesn’t need to be ashamed, properly handling the Word of Truth” (v. 15). The word ὀρθοτομέω means to cut straight. Handling Scripture accurately requires diligence: careful reading, honest interpretation, faithful application. The goal is God's approval, not human applause. Every believer who reads, studies and shares the Bible is called to be this kind of workman.

structure.label: Strong in Grace, Passing It On (v. 1-2)
structure.body: Timothy must be strengthened by grace in Christ and entrust what he heard from Paul to faithful people who will teach others.

structure.label: Soldier, Athlete, Farmer (v. 3-7)
structure.body: Share in suffering like a good soldier who avoids entanglements to please his commander, an athlete who competes by the rules, and a hard-working farmer who first shares the crops; reflect, and the Lord will give understanding.

structure.label: Remember Jesus Christ (v. 8-13)
structure.body: Remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead and descended from David; for this gospel Paul suffers in chains, but God's word is not chained; he endures for the elect's salvation; the faithful saying: dying with Him we live, enduring we reign, denying Him we are denied, faithless He remains faithful.

structure.label: An Approved Workman (v. 14-19)
structure.body: Avoid quarrels about words; be an approved workman who rightly handles the word of truth; avoid empty chatter that spreads like gangrene, as with Hymenaeus and Philetus who say the resurrection has already happened; yet God's firm foundation stands with its seal: the Lord knows those who are His, and those who name Him must turn from unrighteousness.

structure.label: A Vessel for Honour, a Gentle Servant (v. 20-26)
structure.body: In a great house there are vessels for honour and dishonour; whoever cleanses himself will be a vessel for honour, useful to the Master; flee youthful passions and pursue righteousness, faith, love and peace; avoid foolish controversies; the Lord's servant must be gentle, able to teach and patient, correcting opponents with gentleness so that God may grant them repentance and they may escape the devil's snare.

sections.heading: Strength, Succession and Single-Mindedness
paragraphs: Chapter 1 ended with the painful news that many had deserted Paul. Chapter 2 begins, “You therefore, my child, be strengthened in the grace that is in Christ Jesus” (v. 1). Against the background of desertion, Timothy must stand — and his strength must come from grace. Then comes the plan for the gospel's future: “The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also” (v. 2). This is Paul's succession plan. Not a building, not an institution, but faithful people teaching faithful people.

Paul then gives three pictures of faithful ministry. The soldier: “You therefore must endure hardship, as a good soldier of Christ Jesus. No soldier on duty entangles himself in the affairs of life, that he may please him who enrolled him as a soldier” (vv. 3–4). The word for ‘life’ is βίος — ordinary daily business. Not everything ordinary is wrong, but a soldier on campaign must not be entangled by it. The athlete: “Also, if anyone competes in athletics, he isn’t crowned unless he has competed by the rules” (v. 5). The farmer: “The farmer who labors must be the first to get a share of the crops” (v. 6).

Together they teach endurance, integrity and hard work, each with its reward: the commander's approval, the victor's crown, the harvest. Paul does not explain every detail; he tells Timothy, “Consider what I say, and may the Lord give you understanding in all things” (v. 7). Christian understanding comes through reflection and through the Lord's gift together. Paul used the same athletic picture elsewhere: “Don’t you know that those who run in a race all run, but one receives the prize? Run like that, that you may win” (1 Corinthians 9:24).

sections.heading: Remember Jesus Christ
paragraphs: In the middle of the hardship, Paul points Timothy to the centre: “Remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, of the offspring of David, according to my Good News” (v. 8). The resurrection proves that suffering and death are not the end; the descent from David proves that He is the promised King. Paul suffers for this gospel “to the point of chains as a criminal. But God’s word isn’t chained” (v. 9). The authorities can imprison the preacher but not the message. Indeed, Paul's prison letters have reached more people than he could ever have reached in person.

His suffering has a purpose: “Therefore I endure all things for the chosen ones’ sake, that they also may obtain the salvation which is in Christ Jesus with eternal glory” (v. 10). God has chosen people for salvation, and Paul suffers so that the gospel will reach them. Then comes the faithful saying, probably an early Christian hymn: “For if we died with him, we will also live with him. If we endure, we will also reign with him. If we deny him, he also will deny us. If we are faithless, he remains faithful. For he can’t deny himself” (vv. 11–13).

The first two lines are promises: union with Christ in death means life; endurance means reigning with Him. The third is a warning, echoing Jesus: “But whoever denies me before men, him I will also deny before my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 10:33). The fourth is a surprise. We expect ‘if we are faithless, He will be faithless’, but instead: “he remains faithful.” Final, deliberate denial is different from the weak, wavering faith of a struggling believer. Christ's faithfulness does not depend on ours; it rests on His own unchanging character. As Paul asked, “Will their lack of faith nullify the faithfulness of God?” (Romans 3:3).

sections.heading: Rightly Handling the Word
paragraphs: Timothy must remind the believers of these truths and warn them not to “argue about words, to no profit, to the subverting of those who hear” (v. 14). Instead, he must focus on his own work: “Give diligence to present yourself approved by God, a workman who doesn’t need to be ashamed, properly handling the Word of Truth” (v. 15). The picture is of cutting straight. False teachers twisted Scripture; Timothy must handle it honestly and accurately. The approval that matters is God's.

False teaching spreads like disease: “But shun empty chatter, for it will go further in ungodliness, and those words will consume like gangrene” (vv. 16–17). Hymenaeus and Philetus had “erred concerning the truth, saying that the resurrection is already past, and overthrowing the faith of some” (v. 18). They probably taught that resurrection was merely spiritual and had already happened, denying the future bodily resurrection that Paul defended in 1 Corinthians 15. Yet Paul is not shaken: “However God’s firm foundation stands, having this seal, ‘The Lord knows those who are his,’ and, ‘Let every one who names the name of the Lord depart from unrighteousness’” (v. 19). God knows His own; His own turn from sin.

The chapter closes with a picture and a portrait. The picture: a great house with valuable and common vessels, some for honour and some for dishonour. “If anyone therefore purges himself from these, he will be a vessel for honor, sanctified, and suitable for the master’s use, prepared for every good work” (v. 21). The portrait: “The Lord’s servant must not quarrel, but be gentle towards all, able to teach, patient, in gentleness correcting those who oppose him: perhaps God may give them repentance leading to a full knowledge of the truth” (vv. 24–25). Firm in truth, gentle in manner, hopeful for opponents — because they are captives of the devil who need to be set free (v. 26).

ntConnection.heading: Union With Christ and Gentle Correction
paragraphs: The faithful saying of verses 11–13 rests on Paul's teaching about union with Christ: “But if we died with Christ, we believe that we will also live with him” (Romans 6:8). The warning about denial echoes Jesus' own words in Matthew 10:33. And the promise that Christ remains faithful echoes Romans 3:3–4: God's faithfulness is not cancelled by human unfaithfulness — “let God be found true, but every man a liar” (Romans 3:4).

The seal ‘The Lord knows those who are his’ echoes Jesus the Good Shepherd: “I am the good shepherd. I know my own, and I’m known by my own” (John 10:14). The false teaching about the resurrection is the same error Paul confronted in Corinth: “Now if Christ is preached, that he has been raised from the dead, how do some among you say that there is no resurrection of the dead?” (1 Corinthians 15:12).

Paul's call to gentle correction matches his teaching to the Galatians: “Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness” (Galatians 6:1). Repentance is God's gift, as Romans says: “the goodness of God leads you to repentance” (Romans 2:4). And the captivity of unbelievers is described in 2 Corinthians: “the god of this world has blinded the minds of the unbelieving” (2 Corinthians 4:4). Gentle truth-telling is one of God's means of setting captives free.

lexicon.insight: Strong's: “to entwine, i.e. (figuratively) involve with.” The apostle Peter uses the same verb of people ‘entangled’ again in the world's defilements (2 Peter 2:20). In verse 4 it describes a soldier wrapped up in civilian business. The issue is not that the affairs of life are evil, but that they can tangle around a believer's feet and slow the mission. Ask not only ‘Is this wrong?’ but ‘Is this entangling me?’

Strong's: “to bind (in various applications, literally or figuratively).” Paul is chained ‘as a criminal’, but ‘God's word isn't chained’. The contrast is the heart of the verse. Throughout history, governments have imprisoned preachers and banned Bibles, yet the word has kept spreading. You may feel limited by circumstances, but God's word in your mouth and life is never bound.

Strong's: “properly, acceptable (current after assayal), i.e. approved.” It describes a coin that has been tested and found genuine, accepted as currency. The related verb δοκιμάζω means to test (1 Thessalonians 2:4). Timothy must aim to stand before God as a workman whose work passes inspection. The goal is not human approval or popularity but God's verdict: ‘tested and genuine’.

This word appears only here in the New Testament. It combines ὀρθός, straight, and τέμνω, to cut. In the Greek Old Testament it is used of God making straight paths (Proverbs 3:6; 11:5). It may picture a road-builder cutting a straight road, a mason cutting stone true, or a farmer ploughing a straight furrow. Handling God's word rightly means teaching it accurately, without twisting it, so that people can walk straight in it.

Strong's: “enduring of ill, i.e. forbearing.” It appears only here in the New Testament. It combines ἀνέχομαι, to bear with, and κακός, evil: one who bears wrong without becoming bitter. The Lord's servant will be wronged, misunderstood and opposed. Instead of fighting back, he bears it patiently, correcting gently in the hope that God will grant repentance.

holySpiritRevelation.intro: The Spirit is dealing with three things in this chapter: who you are passing the faith to, what is entangling you, and how you handle those who oppose you.

items.title: Who Is Your Faithful Person?
items.body: Paul's succession plan was simple: entrust the gospel to faithful people who will teach others. The Spirit asks: who is your ‘faithful person’? Is there someone younger in faith you are investing in, teaching, encouraging and walking with? If not, ask Him to show you one person. The gospel moves forward one faithful life at a time.

items.title: What Has Entangled You?
items.body: A soldier on duty does not get tangled in civilian affairs. The Spirit may be showing you something good in itself — a hobby, a business opportunity, entertainment, a relationship, a busy schedule — that has wrapped itself around your feet and slowed your obedience. Ask Him: ‘What is entangling me?’ Then decide whether to cut it loose or put it in its proper place.

items.title: Gentle With Opponents
items.body: The Lord's servant must not quarrel but be gentle, patient and hopeful toward opponents. The Spirit may be convicting you about a harsh tone, an argumentative spirit, or a desire to win debates rather than people. Remember that opponents may be captives of the enemy. Ask the Spirit to give you gentleness, and pray that God will grant them repentance.

audit.title: The Relay Check
audit.body: Write down who passed the faith to you, and who you are passing it to (v. 2). If the second line is empty, ask God for one name this week.

audit.title: The Entanglement Check
audit.body: List the main activities that take your time and energy. Circle any that entangle you and distract you from pleasing Christ (v. 4). Choose one to limit.

audit.title: The Handling Check
audit.body: When you share Scripture, do you handle it accurately and in context (v. 15)? Or do you sometimes use verses to support what you already wanted to say? Ask God to make you an honest workman with His word.

practices.title: Start a Relay
practices.body: Choose one person who is newer in faith and invite them to meet with you regularly for the next three months — weekly or fortnightly. Read a book of the Bible together (2 Timothy is ideal), share what you are learning, and pray together. Encourage them, from the beginning, to think about who they will one day pass the faith on to. Paul's plan works one person at a time.

practices.title: Cut It Straight
practices.body: Practise ‘rightly handling the word of truth’ this week. Take one passage — for example 2 Timothy 2:1–13 — and study it carefully: read it several times, note the context, look up key words, ask what it meant to Timothy before asking what it means for you. Write a short summary in your own words. Then share one true, accurate insight from it with someone else.

prayerReflection: “Lord Jesus, strengthen me in the grace that is in You. Help me pass on what I have received to faithful people who will teach others also. Make me a good soldier who endures hardship and is not entangled in the affairs of life, so that I may please You who enlisted me. Make me an athlete who competes by the rules, and a hard-working farmer who waits patiently for the harvest. I remember You, Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, descended from David. Thank You that Your word is not chained. Help me endure everything for the sake of those You have chosen. If I have died with You, I will live with You; if I endure, I will reign with You; keep me from ever denying You; and thank You that even when I am faithless, You remain faithful, because You cannot deny Yourself. Make me a workman approved by God, who handles Your word of truth accurately. Keep me from quarrels about words and empty chatter. Cleanse me, so that I may be a vessel for honour, set apart and useful to You, ready for every good work. Help me flee youthful passions and pursue righteousness, faith, love and peace. Make me gentle, patient and able to teach, correcting others with gentleness, hoping that You will grant them repentance and set them free. In the mighty name of Jesus, Amen!”

storyConnections.title: Elijah Passes the Mantle to Elisha
storyConnections.summary: As the time came for Elijah to be taken up to heaven, his servant Elisha refused to leave him, following him from Gilgal to Bethel to Jericho to the Jordan. Elijah struck the river with his cloak and they crossed on dry ground. Elisha asked for a double portion of Elijah's spirit. A chariot of fire appeared, and Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven. Elisha picked up Elijah's fallen mantle, struck the Jordan and cried, ‘Where is the LORD, the God of Elijah?’ The waters parted again, and the prophets watching said that the spirit of Elijah rested on Elisha. Like Paul handing the deposit to Timothy, Elijah passed his ministry to the next generation — and God's power continued.

storyConnections.title: Peter Denies and Is Restored
storyConnections.summary: After Peter denied Jesus three times on the night of His arrest, the risen Lord met him on the shore of the Sea of Galilee. Three times Jesus asked Peter whether he loved Him, and three times Peter answered that he did. Each time Jesus gave him a commission: feed My lambs, tend My sheep, feed My sheep. Then He told Peter how he would one day glorify God by his death, and said, ‘Follow Me.’ Peter had been faithless, but Christ remained faithful. This is the hope of 2 Timothy 2:13: our failures do not cancel Christ's faithfulness, and He restores those who return to Him.

storyConnections.title: The Bereans Handle the Word Rightly
storyConnections.summary: When Paul and Silas came to Berea after fleeing Thessalonica, they preached in the synagogue. The Bereans were more noble-minded than those in Thessalonica, because they received the message with great eagerness and examined the Scriptures every day to see whether what Paul said was true. As a result, many of them believed. The Bereans show what it means to handle the word of truth rightly: eager to hear, careful to check, ready to obey. Every believer can be this kind of workman.
